title: Which SOLID principles matter most in LLD — Single Responsibility (one class, one job), Open/Closed (extend behavior without modifying existing code), Liskov Substitution (child can replace parent), Dependency Inversion (depend on abstractions, not concrete classes)?
shortTitle: Which SOLID principles matter most in LLD?

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** SOLID is a set of five object-oriented design principles — Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, and Dependency Inversion — that together produce loosely coupled, highly cohesive, and easily extensible code. In day-to-day LLD, Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov, and Dependency Inversion carry the most weight.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of National Bank of India as a well-run branch. Each employee does one job (Single Responsibility). To add a new service, you hire a new specialist rather than retraining everyone (Open/Closed). Any trained teller can replace another without breaking the queue (Liskov). And the manager gives instructions to a "role" like teller, not to a specific person named Rajesh, so anyone filling that role works (Dependency Inversion).

**One line to remember:** SOLID keeps each class focused, extendable without edits, substitutable, and dependent on abstractions.

sections.s2_technical:
Single Responsibility says a class should have one reason to change. A `TransferService` that also formats emails has two reasons to change; split the email part into `NotificationService`.

Open/Closed says software should be open for extension but closed for modification. You achieve this with abstraction: to add a new interest calculation you add a new class implementing `InterestStrategy`, never editing the existing ones.

```java
interface InterestStrategy { BigDecimal interest(BigDecimal balance); }
class SavingsInterest implements InterestStrategy { public BigDecimal interest(BigDecimal b){ return b.multiply(new BigDecimal("0.04")); } }
```

Liskov Substitution says a subclass must honour the parent's contract so it can replace the parent without surprises. If `Account.debit` never throws for valid input, a `SavingsAccount` must not suddenly throw for the same input.

Interface Segregation says keep interfaces small so classes are not forced to implement unused methods. Dependency Inversion says high-level modules depend on abstractions, not concrete classes, usually achieved with constructor injection so you can swap implementations and mock in tests.

The senior nuance: SOLID is guidance, not religion. Applied mechanically it creates needless interfaces. Applied with judgment it makes banking systems that evolve safely under regulatory change.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The interest module at National Bank of India had a single method with a growing if-else for savings, current, and fixed deposit. Every new product forced edits and re-testing of old code, and bugs crept in. This is exactly what Open/Closed and Dependency Inversion fix.

Problem 2 — The same class also sent SMS alerts, so a change to the SMS vendor risked breaking interest math. This is exactly what Single Responsibility fixes by separating concerns.

The code defines an `InterestStrategy` interface, two implementations, an `InterestService` that depends on the abstraction, and a demo computing interest for Rajesh and Priya.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: Rajesh balance 1000000 with savings strategy, Priya balance 250000 with fixed-deposit strategy.

Step 1: two `InterestService` objects are created, each injected with a different strategy — this is Dependency Inversion in action. Step 2: `savings.annualInterest(1000000)` delegates to `SavingsInterest.interest`, returning 40000. Step 3: `fd.annualInterest(250000)` delegates to `FixedDepositInterest.interest`, returning 17500. Step 4: both results are logged. Adding a new product means adding one class, proving Open/Closed.

```
Oct 31 22:06 INFO SOLID: Rajesh savings interest = 40000.00
Oct 31 22:06 INFO SOLID: Priya FD interest = 17500.00
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  main()
    │ inject strategies (Dependency Inversion)
    ▼
  InterestService(SavingsInterest) ── annualInterest(1000000) ─▶ 40000
  InterestService(FixedDeposit)    ── annualInterest(250000)  ─▶ 17500
    │
    ▼
  log both results
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — SOLID Interest Design ═══

  ┌─ SOLID mapping ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: InterestService only computes interest         │
  │ O: new product = new InterestStrategy impl        │
  │ L: any impl substitutes for the interface         │
  │ D: service depends on InterestStrategy abstraction │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────┐
  │   <<interface>>      │
  │  InterestStrategy    │
  │ + interest(bal):BD   │
  └──────────┬───────────┘
      implements
   ┌──────────┼───────────┐
   ▼                      ▼
  ┌──────────────┐  ┌────────────────────┐
  │SavingsInterest│ │FixedDepositInterest│
  └──────────────┘  └────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────┐
  │   InterestService    │◇── depends on InterestStrategy
  │ - strategy           │
  │ + annualInterest(bal)│
  └──────────────────────┘

  Call Chain:
  1. new InterestService(new SavingsInterest())
  2. annualInterest(1000000) → strategy.interest → 40000
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
SOLID is five principles, and in real low-level design four of them do most of the heavy lifting. Single Responsibility means each class has exactly one reason to change, so I keep interest calculation in an interest service and notifications in a notification service, never mixing them, because a change to the SMS vendor should never risk breaking interest math.

Open/Closed means my code is open for extension but closed for modification. In my banking work, when the bank launches a new deposit product, I add a new strategy class implementing the interest interface rather than editing a growing if-else, so I never re-test and re-risk the existing, regulator-approved logic.

Liskov Substitution means any subclass or implementation must honour the parent's contract, so wherever my service expects an interest strategy, any concrete strategy drops in and behaves correctly without special cases. Dependency Inversion means my high-level service depends on the interest-strategy abstraction, not on a concrete class, which I wire through constructor injection — this makes the service trivial to unit test with a mock strategy.

The fifth principle, Interface Segregation, keeps interfaces small so classes are not forced to implement methods they do not use. The senior insight I bring is that SOLID is judgment, not dogma: applied mechanically it breeds needless interfaces, but applied thoughtfully it let my National Bank of India interest module absorb new products and regulatory changes without destabilising proven code.

---

keyPoints: S: Single Responsibility — one class, one reason to change
O: Open/Closed — open for extension, closed for modification
L: Liskov Substitution — subtypes must be substitutable for base types
I: Interface Segregation — many specific interfaces over one general
D: Dependency Inversion — depend on abstractions, not concrete classes
